results.bodyText: Design and finishes Freestanding bath in a renovation: space, plumbing and cost What a freestanding bath needs in a bathroom renovation - room size, plumbing changes, floor strength, cost range and whether it suits your household. Book a free on-site measure Call 0411 752 334 Published 3 October 2026 Reading time 4 min read The appeal of a freestanding bath A freestanding bath sits away from the wall on its own feet or base. It becomes the centrepiece of the room. The look is open, sculptural and less built-in than a drop-in or alcove bath. Freestanding baths have been the most requested bath style in Sydney renovations for several years. They work in both traditional and modern bathrooms. The practical question is whether your room has the space and plumbing for one. How much room you need A freestanding bath needs clear space around it. The bath itself is typically 1,500 to 1,700 millimetres long and 700 to 800 millimetres wide. You need at least 150 millimetres of clearance on each side and 600 millimetres at one end for access. In practice, the bathroom needs to be roughly 8 square metres or larger to carry a freestanding bath without crowding the rest of the room. A smaller room can hold one, but the shower, vanity and toilet end up squeezed. Our walk-in shower vs bathtub guide covers how to decide between the two when space is tight. mainEntity.name: How much does a heated towel rail cost?

acceptedAnswer.text: A basic electric model starts from about $150. A mid-range stainless steel rail runs $400 to $600. Premium models with brushed finishes and smart timers can reach $1,500 or more. Installation during a renovation is minimal extra cost because the electrician is already on site.

mainEntity.name: Are heated towel rails expensive to run?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Most use 60 to 120 watts, about the same as a light globe. On a timer running a few hours per day, the cost is $10 to $20 per month. Leaving it on all day is wasteful but not expensive.

mainEntity.name: Should I get electric or hydronic?

acceptedAnswer.text: Electric, unless your home already has a hydronic heating system. Adding a hydronic system just for a towel rail is not practical or cost-effective. Electric rails are simple to install, reliable and widely available.

mainEntity.name: Can I add a heated towel rail to an existing bathroom?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, with a plug-in model. It plugs into a standard power point. A hardwired model is better installed during a renovation when the walls are open - retrofitting one into a finished bathroom means chasing cables through the wall or running visible conduit.

mainEntity.name: Do heated towel rails work in summer?

acceptedAnswer.text: They still dry towels, which is useful even in warm weather - damp towels in a humid bathroom grow musty. You can leave the rail off in summer and use it only in the cooler months if you prefer.

In a renovation, installing a heated towel rail is simple because the walls are open and the electrician is already on site. Retrofitting one later means chasing cables through finished walls or running visible conduit. Electric heated towel rails Electric models are the most common type in Australian bathrooms. They plug into a power point or are hardwired into the bathroom circuit. Inside the rail, a heating element warms either a dry rod or a sealed liquid that transfers heat to the bars. Liquid-filled rails hold heat longer after they are switched off. Dry-element rails heat up faster. Both work well. The choice is usually about the model and finish, not the heating method. A basic electric rail starts from around $150. A mid-range stainless steel model with six or seven bars runs about $400 to $600. Premium models with smart controls, timers and brushed finishes can reach $1,500 or more. Hydronic heated towel rails A hydronic rail connects to the home's hot water system. Hot water from the boiler or heat pump circulates through the rail. It works the same way as a hydronic radiator. Hydronic rails are less common in Sydney because most homes do not have a hydronic heating system already installed. Adding one just for a towel rail is not cost-effective. If the home already has hydronic heating, connecting a towel rail is straightforward. Our underfloor heating guide covers a related decision - both add warmth to the bathroom, and the two can work together in a premium build. On a timer that runs for a few hours in the morning and evening, the running cost is $10 to $20 per month. A timer switch is strongly recommended. faq.text: Should I get electric or hydronic? Electric, unless your home already has a hydronic heating system. Adding a hydronic system just for a towel rail is not practical or cost-effective. Electric rails are simple to install, reliable and widely available.

faq.question: Can I add a heated towel rail to an existing bathroom?
faq.text: Can I add a heated towel rail to an existing bathroom? Yes, with a plug-in model. It plugs into a standard power point. A hardwired model is better installed during a renovation when the walls are open - retrofitting one into a finished bathroom means chasing cables through the wall or running visible conduit.

faq.question: Do heated towel rails work in summer?
faq.text: Do heated towel rails work in summer? They still dry towels, which is useful even in warm weather - damp towels in a humid bathroom grow musty. You can leave the rail off in summer and use it only in the cooler months if you prefer.

The wall framing may be hardwood. The drainage may be clay or cast iron. The floor may sit on timber rather than a slab. Lead pipe, old water lines or asbestos may turn up once the room is opened. If the home is heritage-listed or in a heritage area, there are extra approval steps. The good news: most internal bathroom work does not need heritage consent. The real work is in the structure and the services, not the forms. Heritage listing vs heritage conservation area A heritage-listed home is on the NSW Heritage Register or a council list for its own value. A heritage area (HCA) protects the look of a whole street or block. The rules mainly cover changes you can see from outside. For bathroom work, the split matters. A like-for-like internal fit-out - same footprint, same wet area, no walls moved - usually needs no heritage consent under either type. Changes to the outside of the building, to load-bearing walls or to heritage features inside may need a statement and council sign-off. We check this at the on-site measure so the position is clear before the quote is written. What you usually find behind the walls Older Sydney homes share a pattern. The bathroom was often added or last done up decades ago. The pipes, drains and linings behind the walls are from that era. Clay drains crack and sag. Old water pipes corrode and choke flow. Lead lines still turn up in some pre-1950s homes. Fibro sheeting, vinyl tiles and pipe lagging with asbestos are common in homes built before the mid-1980s. None of this is unusual. A builder who works on older homes expects it. The key is that the quote allows for what is likely at strip-out, rather than treating it as a surprise. Our demolition guide covers what the strip-out process looks like step by step. Structural and waterproofing considerations A bathroom on a timber floor needs more prep before it can be sealed. The membrane cannot bridge movement in the subfloor. The base may need to be stiffened or re-sheeted first. This is normal on older homes but adds a step a slab bathroom does not need. Wall framing in older homes is often uneven. Stud spacing, plumb and level can vary. The framing may need packing or new lining before tiles go on. This is prep work, not a defect - it is how these houses were built. Every bathroom we renovate is waterproofed to AS 3740 and issued a compliance certificate, regardless of the age of the home. Designing a bathroom that suits the house A heritage home does not need a heritage-themed bathroom. What it needs is a bathroom that does not fight the character of the house. The proportions, ceiling height, natural light and architectural language of the home should influence the design - not dictate it. A freestanding bath, a frameless shower and modern fittings can work well in a terrace if the scale and palette suit the house. Our Rocks project shows this: large wall tiles, patterned floor tiles, matte black fittings and a freestanding bath sit around the original leadlight window. Period-style fixtures are one approach, but not the only one. A clean, modern bathroom that suits the room often ages better than a mix of heritage copies. Common design choices in older-home bathrooms Subway tiles and hexagonal mosaics reference historical tile formats without committing to a full period reproduction. They work as well in a 1920s bungalow as in a contemporary apartment. Freestanding baths suit rooms with higher ceilings and enough floor area. In a compact bathroom, a built-in bath or a walk-in shower makes better use of the space. Timber vanities or vanities with a timber shelf bring warmth to a tiled room and suit the material palette of most older Sydney homes. Brushed brass and champagne gold fittings complement warm-toned timber and stone without looking out of place in a period home. Cost considerations for older homes A bathroom in an older home can cost more than the same scope in a newer house. The gap is almost always in the prep, not the finishes. Replacing old pipes, fixing a timber floor, removing asbestos and getting the base ready for tiles all add labour and time. The best way to manage this is to allow for it from the start. A quote that assumes the best case behind the walls is a quote that will change at strip-out. We walk through what is likely at the on-site measure and price to match. ETR's packages start from $18,000 for a Basic renovation in a small bathroom. Older homes more commonly fall into the Standard (from $25,000) or Premium (from $30,000) range because of the preparation work involved. itemListElement.name: How long does a bathroom renovation last?

mainEntity.name: How long does bathroom waterproofing last?

acceptedAnswer.text: Waterproofing done to AS 3740 is made to last for the life of the renovation, which is usually 15 to 20 years or more. It fails early only when it is done poorly or damaged by later work.

mainEntity.name: How often should I reseal the silicone in my bathroom?

acceptedAnswer.text: Silicone around the shower and basin usually lasts 5 to 10 years. Redo it sooner if it lifts, splits or goes dark, because a failed seal lets water in behind the tiles.

mainEntity.name: Do bathroom tiles need replacing over time?

acceptedAnswer.text: Good tiles can last 15 to 20 years or more and often outlast the rest of the room. The grout and seals around them wear first, so they are what usually needs attention, not the tiles.

mainEntity.name: Does a bathroom renovation come with a warranty?

acceptedAnswer.text: Ours does. Elite Touch Renovations provides a 10-year workmanship warranty on the work we do. Taps, fans and other fittings carry their own separate maker warranties.

mainEntity.name: What makes a bathroom wear out faster?

acceptedAnswer.text: Trapped damp is the main cause. A weak or missing exhaust fan, poor falls to the drain and failed seals all let moisture sit in the room, which leads to mould and tile and membrane failure.

results.bodyText: Planning and cost How long does a bathroom renovation last? How long a bathroom renovation lasts, what makes one last longer, and why the waterproofing, tiling and ventilation decide its real lifespan. Book a free on-site measure Call 0411 752 334 Published 4 November 2026 Reading time 4 min read Quick answer A well-built bathroom renovation is usually made to last 15 to 20 years or more before it needs major work. The look may be refreshed sooner, but the room underneath should go the distance. What decides this is the work you cannot see once the tiles are on: the waterproofing, the fall of the floor to the drain, the tiling and grout, and the exhaust fan. Get those right and the room lasts. Get them wrong and it fails early, whatever the taps cost. Roughly how long each part of a bathroom lasts when it is done well. Part of the bathroom Typical lifespan Waterproofing Hidden under the tiles. The life of the renovation, done to AS 3740 Tiles and grout Grout may need resealing. 15 to 20 years or more Taps, shower and toilet The working fittings. 10 to 15 years Silicone seals Around the shower and basin. 5 to 10 years, then redone Exhaust fan Clears the damp air. 5 to 10 years These are general guides, not a promise about your room. The firm commitment we make is a 10-year workmanship warranty on the work we do. Book a free on-site measure What makes a bathroom last? The parts that keep water where it belongs are what make a bathroom last: the waterproofing, the way the floor falls to the drain, and a fan that clears the damp air. When these are right, the tiles stay sound and the walls behind them stay dry. Fittings and finishes matter too, but they are the easy part to change later. The hard part to fix is the work sealed under the tiles. That is why a lasting bathroom is decided before the first tile goes on, not at the shop when you pick the taps. mainEntity.name: Do I need a licensed builder for a bathroom renovation in Sydney?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Any home building work over $5,000 in NSW must be done by a licensed contractor. The licence can be checked on the NSW Fair Trading website. Unlicensed work is not covered by the Home Building Fund.

mainEntity.name: How many quotes should I get for a bathroom renovation?

acceptedAnswer.text: Three is the standard advice. More than three makes it harder to compare without adding much clarity. Make sure each quote covers the same scope so you are comparing like for like.

mainEntity.name: What questions should I ask a bathroom renovator before hiring?

acceptedAnswer.text: Ask for their licence number, proof of cover, a written warranty, a detailed quote with what is and is not included, a timeline, a payment schedule, and references from recent projects.

mainEntity.name: How do I check a builder licence in NSW?

acceptedAnswer.text: Go to the NSW Fair Trading website and search by licence number or business name. The search shows the licence type, holder name, status and any conditions. It takes under a minute.

mainEntity.name: What is the Home Building Fund?

acceptedAnswer.text: A government-backed fund that protects homeowners if a licensed builder cannot finish the work or fix defects - for example, if they become insolvent. It applies to home work over $20,000 in NSW. Unlicensed work is not covered.

If a line is vague, ask for it to be made clear in writing. A lower price may cost more if key work has been left for later. What is the risk with a verbal estimate? A verbal estimate can be useful for an early conversation, but it is not enough to sign on. It may not define the tile allowance, fixture choices, access, waste removal, waterproofing, electrical work or what happens if hidden damage is found. The problem is not that every estimate is dishonest. The problem is that an estimate leaves too many assumptions outside the decision, and those assumptions can turn into extra cost once your bathroom is already out of action. What should a fixed-scope quote include? A fixed-scope written quote should say what room is being renovated, what work is included, what is excluded, which selections are allowed for and how variations are approved. It should also show the payment schedule and any program assumptions. For a bathroom, look closely for demolition, plumbing and electrical preparation, waterproofing to AS 3740 , tiling, fit-off, rubbish removal and final clean. If one quote names those items and another does not, you are not comparing the same thing. Check the assumptions Look for assumptions about the room size, tile format, fitting allowances, access, work hours and the state of the walls and floor. These details can change the final result. Ask how changes are priced and approved. You should know who can approve a change and how it will be recorded before work goes ahead. itemListElement.name: Large-format tiles in a bathroom renovation: pros, cons and what to know

mainEntity.name: Are large-format tiles more expensive than standard tiles?

acceptedAnswer.text: The tiles themselves are often the same price per square metre. The cost difference is in installation - large tiles require a flatter substrate, more careful handling, and higher-skill cutting. Labour costs are typically higher, and waste from breakage costs more per tile.

mainEntity.name: Can I use large-format tiles in a small bathroom?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Large tiles can make a small bathroom feel more spacious by reducing grout lines. A 300 by 600 or 600 by 600 tile works well in most small rooms. Very large tiles (600 by 1,200 or bigger) may produce more waste from cuts in a tight space.

mainEntity.name: Can large-format tiles be used on a shower floor?

acceptedAnswer.text: Generally not. Shower floors are graded to a drain, and large tiles cannot follow the gradient without lippage or awkward cuts. Smaller tiles - mosaics or 100 by 100 tiles - follow the fall more easily and provide better grip on a wet surface.

mainEntity.name: What causes lippage with large-format tiles?

acceptedAnswer.text: Lippage happens when one edge of a tile sits higher than the next, usually because the substrate is not flat enough. Large tiles span more surface area, so even small variations in the wall or floor become visible. Proper substrate preparation is the fix.

mainEntity.name: What grout width should I use with large-format tiles?

acceptedAnswer.text: A 1.5 to 2 millimetre grout joint is standard for large-format rectified tiles. Narrower joints emphasise the seamless look. The tile manufacturer specifies the minimum joint width - going below it can cause cracking if the tile or substrate moves.

results.bodyText: Design and finishes Large-format tiles in a bathroom renovation: pros, cons and what to know What to know about using large-format tiles in a bathroom renovation - the look, the installation requirements, the cost and where they work best. Book a free on-site measure Call 0411 752 334 Published 3 October 2026 Reading time 4 min read What counts as a large-format tile A large-format tile is any tile where one side is 400 millimetres or longer. Common bathroom sizes are 300 by 600, 600 by 600 and 600 by 1,200 millimetres. Some suppliers now offer 800 by 1,600 and even 1,200 by 1,200 panels for feature walls. The trend toward larger tiles has been building for years. Fewer grout lines give the room a cleaner, more seamless look and make the space feel larger. But larger tiles bring specific installation requirements that smaller tiles do not. The visual advantage Fewer grout lines mean less visual interruption. A wall covered in 600 by 1,200 tiles reads as a continuous surface rather than a grid. In a small bathroom, this effect makes the room feel more spacious. Large-format tiles also show the tile pattern - veining, texture, colour variation - more clearly. A marble-look porcelain tile at 600 by 1,200 displays the veining across a single piece rather than cutting it into small fragments. The result looks more natural and less repetitive. Our colour schemes guide covers how tile format and colour work together to set the room's tone. Installation requirements Large tiles need a flat substrate. Even a slight variation in the wall or floor surface - 2 to 3 millimetres over a metre - causes lippage, where one edge of the tile sits higher than the next. The substrate must be prepared to a tighter tolerance than for smaller tiles. The adhesive matters. Large tiles need a high-bond, flexible tile adhesive applied with a notched trowel in a pattern that ensures full coverage across the back of the tile. Spot-fixing - applying adhesive in dabs - risks voids under the tile, which can crack under load or movement. Cutting large-format tiles requires a tile saw large enough to handle the size. Curved cuts, around pipes and drains, are harder and produce more waste. Plan on ordering 15 to 20 percent more tiles than the measured area to account for cuts and breakage. Where large-format tiles work best Feature walls. A single wall behind the vanity or in the shower recess in a large-format tile creates a focal point. The rest of the room can use a simpler, smaller tile to balance the visual weight. Floor tiles in open areas. A 600 by 600 or 600 by 1,200 tile on the floor of a larger bathroom reduces grout lines and is easy to clean. In a compact bathroom, a single row of 600 by 1,200 tiles may be all the floor needs. Wall tiles in showers. Large tiles on the shower walls reduce the grout area, which reduces the surface that needs regular sealing and cleaning. A shower with four large tiles per wall looks cleaner than one with twenty small tiles. Where they are harder to use Shower floors. The floor of a walk-in shower is graded to a drain. A large tile cannot follow a multi-directional gradient without either lippage or visible cuts. Shower floors suit smaller tiles - mosaics or 100 by 100 tiles - that follow the curve of the fall. Small rooms with many fixtures. A bathroom with a toilet, vanity, shower recess and door frame in a tight space has many cuts and junctions. Large tiles mean more waste and more complex cutting around obstacles. Curved or uneven walls. Older homes with walls that are not plumb or flat need more preparation before large tiles can go on. The cost of straightening the substrate can offset the savings from fewer tiles. Cost considerations Large-format tiles are not always more expensive per square metre than smaller tiles. Many popular porcelain ranges cost the same across sizes. The cost difference is in the installation - large tiles take more time to handle, more care to set and more skill to cut. Labour costs are typically higher for large-format tiles because the tiler works more slowly to get the substrate right, handle the tiles without breaking them, and achieve a flat, lippage-free finish. A 600 by 1,200 tile that cracks during cutting wastes eight times the material of a 300 by 300 tile. The total cost depends on the room size, the tile size, the number of cuts and the substrate condition. ETR's on-site measure confirms what is practical and quotes accordingly. How ETR handles large-format tiles Large-format tiles are selected during the planning phase, before the quote is finalised. The tile choice affects the substrate preparation, the adhesive specification and the tiling time. The written quote accounts for these requirements. Adam Dawood has over 25 years in tiling and project management. The team handles large-format tiles regularly, including full-height feature walls and floor-to-ceiling shower tiles. Every bathroom is waterproofed to AS 3740 with a compliance certificate. A free on-site measure anywhere in Sydney is the starting point. itemListElement.name: Porcelain vs ceramic tiles for a bathroom: which is better?

mainEntity.name: Is porcelain always better than ceramic for a bathroom?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not always. Porcelain is the stronger choice for floors and wet areas. On walls, ceramic works well and often costs less. The best plan can use both.

mainEntity.name: Is porcelain more expensive than ceramic?

acceptedAnswer.text: Usually, but not always. Porcelain is harder to cut, so labour can also cost more. Both groups range from budget to premium, so compare the exact tile.

mainEntity.name: Can I use ceramic tiles on a bathroom floor?

acceptedAnswer.text: You can, if the tile is rated for floors and has a suitable slip rating. Porcelain is the more common choice because it is harder and absorbs less water.

mainEntity.name: What is a through-body porcelain tile?

acceptedAnswer.text: It is a porcelain tile with the same colour all the way through. A chip shows the same colour as the surface, so damage is less obvious than on a glazed tile with a different body colour.

mainEntity.name: Do porcelain tiles need sealing?

acceptedAnswer.text: Many glazed porcelain tiles do not need sealing, but the grout and some natural-look or unglazed tiles may. Follow the maker advice for the exact product you choose.

faq.text: Is porcelain more expensive than ceramic? Usually, but not always. Porcelain is harder to cut, so labour can also cost more. Both groups range from budget to premium, so compare the exact tile.

faq.question: Can I use ceramic tiles on a bathroom floor?
faq.text: Can I use ceramic tiles on a bathroom floor? You can, if the tile is rated for floors and has a suitable slip rating. Porcelain is the more common choice because it is harder and absorbs less water.

faq.question: What is a through-body porcelain tile?
faq.text: What is a through-body porcelain tile? It is a porcelain tile with the same colour all the way through. A chip shows the same colour as the surface, so damage is less obvious than on a glazed tile with a different body colour.

faq.question: Do porcelain tiles need sealing?
faq.text: Do porcelain tiles need sealing? Many glazed porcelain tiles do not need sealing, but the grout and some natural-look or unglazed tiles may. Follow the maker advice for the exact product you choose.

results.bodyText: Choosing a renovator How to choose a bathroom renovator in Sydney without getting burned The questions that help Sydney homeowners check licensing, scope, communication, waterproofing, timing and aftercare before choosing a renovator. Book a free on-site measure Call 0411 752 334 Published 10 September 2026 Reading time 4 min read Questions about the company Ask who holds the licence, who will manage the project and who will be your day-to-day contact. Confirm the business name on the quote matches the business you are engaging. For ETR, the NSW Builder Licence is 475204C. The project is run by the Dawood family, with Omar Dawood as Licensed Builder and Civil Engineer and Adam Dawood as Licensed Tiler and Projects Manager. Questions about the work Ask what is included in demolition, plumbing, electrical work, waterproofing, tiling, fittings, waste removal and clean-up. Ask how the team deals with changes or hidden conditions. You should also ask how the renovation will be sequenced, what decisions are needed before work begins and how the team will protect the rest of your home. Questions that reveal a hard sell Be careful when a renovator pushes for a decision before measuring the room, avoids writing down exclusions or says a bathroom can be priced from photos alone. A confident builder should be able to explain what is known and what still needs checking. Ask why the quoted program is realistic, what could change it and how product delays are handled. A vague answer now usually becomes stress later. Questions about waterproofing and paperwork Ask how the bathroom will be waterproofed, what standard applies and whether a certificate is supplied. For ETR bathroom renovations, waterproofing is done to AS 3740 with primer plus two coats, and a compliance certificate is supplied. Ask what other handover documents you should keep with the final scope, warranty terms and product information. A careful paper trail is not exciting, but it matters if you ever need to check what was agreed. Questions about the quote and warranty Ask for a fixed-scope written quote , the payment schedule, the variation process and the terms of any warranty. Make sure the warranty wording is specific and do not assume it covers third-party fittings unless the terms say so. A good first conversation should leave you with fewer assumptions, not more. If the answer changes depending on who you speak to, ask for the agreed position in writing. How should you decide after the answers? Compare the written scope, not just the price. The right renovator should be clear about what is included, who is on site, how updates are handled and what happens if the old room hides a problem. You are choosing the people who will have your bathroom open for weeks. Good communication, clean site habits and a clear variation process are not extras; they are part of the job. What proof should matter most? Look for checkable proof: a licence number, a written quote, clear waterproofing paperwork, a real warranty and real customer feedback. Vague claims about quality are not the same as evidence. For ETR, the load-bearing trust signals are plain: NSW Builder Licence 475204C, AS 3740 waterproofing, fixed-scope written quotes, a free on-site measure and a 10-year workmanship warranty stated as written. What should make you pause? Pause if the scope is hard to understand, the price keeps changing without written detail or the renovator avoids basic questions about timing, waterproofing and variations. A bathroom renovation is too disruptive to run on guesswork. If the conversation feels rushed before you sign, it rarely becomes clearer after demolition. What should feel clear before you say yes? You should know who you call, what happens first, what the written quote includes, when the bathroom will be out of action and how changes are approved. If those answers are clear, the decision becomes less about trusting a sales pitch and more about choosing the team with the cleanest process. mainEntity.name: Can I just replace the tiles and keep the rest?

acceptedAnswer.text: Only if the waterproofing under them is sound. New tiles over a failed seal will leak again, because the problem is the layer beneath, not the tiles. Lifting the tiles is also when hidden damage is usually found.

mainEntity.name: How do I know if my bathroom waterproofing has failed?

acceptedAnswer.text: The common signs are water stains on the ceiling in the room below, a musty smell, bubbling paint on the far side of a shower wall, or tiles sounding hollow. Any of these means water is getting past the seal.

mainEntity.name: Is it cheaper to repair or replace a bathroom?

acceptedAnswer.text: A single repair is cheaper than a renovation. But repeated repairs on a failing room often cost more over time than one rebuild, because the underlying problem keeps coming back.

mainEntity.name: How old should a bathroom be before you renovate?

acceptedAnswer.text: There is no set age. Many bathrooms are renovated at 15 to 20 years, but the trigger is the condition, not the age. A sound older bathroom can be left, and a poorly built newer one may need replacing sooner.

mainEntity.name: Why does mould keep coming back in my bathroom?

acceptedAnswer.text: Usually because damp is not clearing. A weak or missing exhaust fan, poor ventilation or a failed seal lets moisture sit in the room. Cleaning treats the surface, but the damp has to be fixed to stop it returning.

Replace the bathroom when the problem is in the structure or spread across the room: failed waterproofing, a floor that moves, mould that keeps coming back, or a layout that no longer works. Repair when it is one fitting, a cracked tile or a worn seal.

The deciding question is the waterproofing. Once the seal under the tiles has failed, there is no lasting fix without lifting the floor, and at that point a full renovation is usually the better spend.
Not sure which you need? A free on-site measure tells you whether a repair will hold or the room needs rebuilding.

Replace the room when the problems are spread out or sit in the structure. Failed waterproofing, a floor that flexes or moves, mould you cannot get rid of, and tiles coming away in more than one spot all point past a repair.

The clearest sign you need to replace rather than repair is water showing up where it should not: stains on the ceiling in the room below, a musty smell, or paint bubbling on the other side of a shower wall. These mean the seal under the tiles has failed.

itemListElement.name: Shower screens explained: frameless, semi-frameless and framed

mainEntity.name: Are frameless shower screens worth the extra cost?

acceptedAnswer.text: In a small bathroom, yes - the visual difference is significant. A frameless screen makes the room feel more open and is easier to clean. In a larger bathroom with a separate shower recess, the difference is less noticeable, and a semi-frameless screen may be a better value.

mainEntity.name: How thick should shower screen glass be?

acceptedAnswer.text: Frameless screens use 10-millimetre toughened safety glass. Semi-frameless screens use 6 to 8-millimetre glass. Framed screens use 4 to 6-millimetre glass. Thicker glass is heavier and more expensive, but it does not flex or rattle.

mainEntity.name: Can I put a shower screen in a wet room?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, but many wet room designs use a fixed glass panel instead of a full screen with a door. The panel acts as a splash guard while keeping the open, walk-in feel. The floor is graded to a drain, so water is managed by the fall, not the screen.

mainEntity.name: How do I stop water marks on a frameless screen?

acceptedAnswer.text: A squeegee after each shower removes most water before it dries. A weekly clean with white vinegar or a glass cleaner removes mineral deposits. Some screens come with a nano-coating that makes water bead and run off, reducing spots.

mainEntity.name: What colour frames are available?

acceptedAnswer.text: The most common finishes are chrome, matt black, brushed nickel and brushed gold. Matt black is the most popular in current Sydney renovations. The frame colour should match or complement the tapware and towel rail finishes in the room.

results.bodyText: Design and finishes Shower screens explained: frameless, semi-frameless and framed The three main types of shower screen - frameless, semi-frameless and framed - compared on cost, cleaning, installation and which suits your bathroom renovation. Book a free on-site measure Call 0411 752 334 Published 3 October 2026 Updated 2 November 2026 Reading time 4 min read Why the shower screen matters The shower screen is one of the most visible elements in a bathroom. It sits at eye level, it is the first thing you touch in the morning, and it determines how much light passes through the shower recess. The wrong screen makes a small bathroom feel smaller. The right one opens the room up. There are three main types: frameless, semi-frameless and framed. Each has a different look, a different price point and different installation needs. If you are down to two, see our frameless vs semi-frameless comparison . Frameless shower screens A frameless screen uses panels of 10-millimetre toughened safety glass held by minimal brackets and hinges. There is no metal frame around the edges. The result is a clean, open look that lets light through and makes the bathroom feel larger. Cleaning is easier because there are no channels or frame edges to trap soap scum. A squeegee after each shower and a weekly wipe keeps the glass clear. The trade-off is cost and precision. Frameless screens need walls that are straight and plumb. If the walls are out of square - common in older Sydney homes - the glass panel will not sit flush, and the gap lets water through. Wall preparation before installation adds to the cost. Expect to pay $800 to $2,000 or more for a frameless screen, depending on the size and configuration. Semi-frameless shower screens A semi-frameless screen frames the fixed panels but leaves the door edge largely unframed. It uses 6 to 8-millimetre toughened glass. The frame at the top and bottom provides structure, while the unframed door keeps a clean look. This is the middle ground. It costs less than frameless, tolerates walls that are slightly out of square, and still looks current. Most mid-range bathroom renovations in Sydney use a semi-frameless screen. Cleaning is a little more work than frameless - the frame channels collect some residue - but less than a fully framed screen. Framed shower screens A framed screen has an aluminium or steel frame around every panel and uses 4 to 6-millimetre glass. It is the most forgiving on walls that are not perfectly level and the most affordable option. The frame channels collect soap scum and mineral deposits. Regular cleaning with a mould-resistant bathroom cleaner keeps them in good condition, but they require more attention than frameless glass. Framed screens suit tight budgets and older homes where wall straightening would add too much cost. They are functional, durable and still available in modern finishes - matt black, brushed nickel and chrome. Sliding, hinged and fixed panels The screen type and the door type are separate choices. A frameless screen can have a hinged door, a pivot door or a fixed panel with an open entry. A framed screen can have a sliding door - useful in small bathrooms where a swinging door would hit the vanity or toilet. Sliding doors suit tight spaces. Hinged doors open wider and are easier to clean. Fixed panels with no door at all are used in walk-in and wet room designs where the shower is open to the room. Which screen suits your renovation In a small bathroom, a frameless fixed panel with an open entry makes the room feel bigger than a framed sliding door. In a large bathroom, a frameless hinged door is the clean, premium choice. In a budget renovation, a semi-frameless or framed screen delivers a good result without the wall preparation cost. The choice also depends on the tile and tapware finishes. Our colour schemes guide covers how the screen frame colour ties into the room's palette - matt black frames with dark tapware, for example, or chrome frames in a lighter scheme. How ETR handles shower screens The shower screen is selected during the design phase, after the layout is settled. Farah Dawood, our architectural designer, helps choose a screen that suits the room size, tile layout and budget. The screen is measured and ordered after tiling is complete, so the fit is precise. Every shower recess is waterproofed to AS 3740 before the screen goes in. A free on-site measure anywhere in Sydney is the starting point. A frameless screen makes the room feel more open and is easier to clean. The shower screen is selected during the design phase, after the layout is settled. Farah Dawood, our architectural designer, helps choose a screen that suits the room size, tile layout and budget. The screen is measured and ordered after tiling is complete, so the fit is precise.
Every shower recess is waterproofed to AS 3740 before the screen goes in. A free on-site measure anywhere in Sydney is the starting point.

In a small bathroom, yes - the visual difference is significant. A frameless screen makes the room feel more open and is easier to clean. In a larger bathroom with a separate shower recess, the difference is less noticeable, and a semi-frameless screen may be a better value.

Frameless screens use 10-millimetre toughened safety glass. Semi-frameless screens use 6 to 8-millimetre glass. Framed screens use 4 to 6-millimetre glass. Thicker glass is heavier and more expensive, but it does not flex or rattle.

Yes, but many wet room designs use a fixed glass panel instead of a full screen with a door. The panel acts as a splash guard while keeping the open, walk-in feel. The floor is graded to a drain, so water is managed by the fall, not the screen.

A squeegee after each shower removes most water before it dries. A weekly clean with white vinegar or a glass cleaner removes mineral deposits. Some screens come with a nano-coating that makes water bead and run off, reducing spots.

The most common finishes are chrome, matt black, brushed nickel and brushed gold. Matt black is the most popular in current Sydney renovations. The frame colour should match or complement the tapware and towel rail finishes in the room.

It is not only for people with limited mobility. A built-in bench makes shaving legs easier, gives children a place to sit, and turns a daily shower into a more relaxed experience. Planning a seat during the renovation is far cheaper than adding one later. A built-in bench costs $300 to $800 when installed during the tiling phase. Retrofitting one into a finished shower is costly and may compromise the sealing. Built-in bench seats A built-in bench is a tiled ledge that forms part of the shower wall. It is fully waterproofed and tiled to match the rest of the shower. The standard size is 400 to 500 millimetres deep, 450 to 500 millimetres high, and at least 600 millimetres wide. Built-in benches look seamless and do not take up floor space the way a freestanding stool does. They are the most popular choice in mid-range to premium bathroom renovations. Our niche and recess guide covers how built-in elements are waterproofed. Fold-down and wall-mounted seats A fold-down seat mounts to the wall and folds flat when not in use. It is a good option when the shower is too narrow for a built-in bench. Stainless steel and teak are the most common materials. These seats need solid mounting - a stud or timber blocking behind the tiles, not just plasterboard. If the seat is planned during the renovation, the builder installs the blocking while the walls are open. Our aging-in-place guide explains blocking in detail. Freestanding shower stools A freestanding stool or chair can be added to any shower at any time. No building work is needed. Teak, bamboo, and medical-grade plastic are common materials. The trade-off is that stools take up floor space, can move when wet, and do not match the look of a tiled shower as well as a built-in bench does. They are best as a short-term solution or in a rental property. Sizing and placement The shower must be large enough to fit a seat and still have room to stand and move. A shower with a built-in bench should be at least 1,200 by 900 millimetres. The bench is usually placed on the wall opposite the shower head. Height matters for comfort. A seat height of 450 to 500 millimetres suits most adults. For someone in a wheelchair who transfers to the seat, 450 millimetres matches the chair height. Universal design and future-proofing A shower seat is one of the simplest universal design features. results.bodyText: Planning and process Renovating a bathroom in a Sydney apartment or strata unit? Bathroom renovations in Sydney apartments and strata units need owners corporation approval, by-law checks and wet-area sign-off before work starts. Book a free on-site measure Call 0411 752 334 Published 10 September 2026 Updated 2 November 2026 Reading time 4 min read The short version Renovating a bathroom in a Sydney apartment or strata unit starts with the building rules. A wet-area renovation is not the same as a cosmetic refresh inside a free-standing house. Does a strata bathroom renovation need approval? Yes. NSW Government guidance says a renovation that requires waterproofing cannot be treated as minor cosmetic work, so get the owners corporation's approval before work starts. Depending on the scope, approval may need a special resolution; work that changes common property may also need a by-law. Check your scheme's rules and approval path before setting a start date. Read the NSW Government strata renovations guidance and confirm the requirements with your strata manager. What we handle for strata jobs The written scope sets out the agreed renovation work. It is carried out under NSW Builder Licence 475204C, and the waterproofing is completed to AS 3740 with a compliance certificate. Give your renovator the approval conditions and building rules so the written scope can reflect them. Your owners corporation or strata manager can confirm which rules apply to your building. What should you ask strata before the quote? Ask if the owners corporation needs a renovation application, which forms they need, what work hours apply, how to book the lift and whether shared areas need special protection. Ask for the rules in writing. A neighbour may help, but the renovator needs the building rules before the work plan and quote are final. Plan access and protection Check how materials and waste can move through the building, where trucks can stop and how shared areas must be kept safe. These details belong in the work plan and quote. Give the team the building rules early so the site plan fits the property. A good access plan is part of the job, not an afterthought. Why access can affect timing Apartment work can take longer when lifts, loading zones, parking, concierge rules or waste removal windows are tight. None of those details changes the quality of the bathroom, but they can change the way the job is staged. This is why a strata renovation should not be priced as if it were a freestanding house with easy driveway access. The access plan is part of the scope. Keep the paperwork together Keep approvals, the written scope, choices, certificates and records of changes in one place. Clear records help everyone see what was agreed. A free on-site measure is a good first step before we write a strata quote. If you are comparing a unit renovation with a house renovation, read our apartment bathroom renovation vs house guide next. What should not be assumed? Do not assume the work can start just because the renovation is inside your apartment. Also do not assume every building has the same approval steps. Older blocks, newer buildings and tightly managed strata schemes can all handle wet-area work differently. Bring the building rules to the first serious quote conversation. That gives the renovator a fair basis for scope, timing and access, and it gives you fewer surprises once the bathroom is open. How should neighbours and common areas be handled? A strata bathroom renovation is not only about your apartment. Noise , lift use, hallway protection and waste movement can affect neighbours and common property. Ask how notices, access windows and protection are handled in your building. The smoother those details are, the less likely the job is to stall over something that was known before work started. What should you give the renovator? Give the renovator the by-laws, approval conditions, contact details for the building manager and any forms the building wants completed. Those documents shape access and timing as much as the bathroom design does. If the building changes a rule after the quote, ask for the timing and cost effect to be recorded before the plan changes. That is the safest way to keep a renovation moving without surprises. Who writes these guides Elite Touch Renovations is a family business in Sydney. itemListElement.name: Toilet upgrades during a bathroom renovation: types, costs and what to know

mainEntity.name: Which toilet type is easiest to clean?

acceptedAnswer.text: Wall-hung, because the pan is off the floor and you can mop underneath. Back to wall is a close second - no gaps behind the pan. Close coupled is the hardest because of the join between the cistern and the bowl.

mainEntity.name: How much does a new toilet cost in a bathroom renovation?

acceptedAnswer.text: Supply plus fitting: $600 to $1,100 for a close coupled, $900 to $1,700 for a back to wall, and $1,500 to $3,300 for a wall-hung with concealed frame. These are typical ranges for mid-quality Australian brands.

mainEntity.name: Can I change from a close coupled toilet to a wall-hung?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, but it requires changes to the plumbing and wall framing. A concealed cistern frame must be installed inside the wall cavity. This is easiest during a full renovation when the walls are already open.

mainEntity.name: What WELS rating should I look for in a toilet?

acceptedAnswer.text: A 4-star dual-flush model is the current standard. It uses about 4.5 litres on a full flush and 3 litres on a half flush. Some 5-star models use even less water.

mainEntity.name: Do wall-hung toilets hold the weight of a heavy person?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. A properly installed wall-hung toilet with a certified mounting frame holds 400 kilograms or more. The frame is bolted into the wall studs and floor, not just the plasterboard.

Book a free on-site measure Call 0411 752 334 Published 3 October 2026 Updated 2 November 2026 Reading time 4 min read Why the toilet matters in a renovation The toilet is the most-used fixture in the bathroom. Yet it is often the last thing people think about during a renovation. Choosing the right type affects the look of the room, how easy it is to clean, and how much water the household uses. A new toilet suite costs $400 to $2,500 depending on the type and brand. The fitting cost is $200 to $600. Given that the toilet will be used ten to fifteen thousand times a year, it is worth getting right. Back to wall toilets A back to wall toilet sits flush against the wall. The cistern is hidden - either in the wall cavity or inside a furniture unit. The result is a clean, modern look with no exposed pipes or tanks. These are the most popular choice in Australian bathroom renovations in 2026. They are easy to clean because there are no gaps behind the pan where dust and grime collect. They suit most bathroom sizes and styles. Wall-hung toilets A wall-hung toilet is mounted on the wall, with the pan off the floor. The cistern is concealed inside the wall. This creates a floating look and makes it very easy to clean the floor beneath. Wall-hung toilets need a strong mounting frame inside the wall cavity, which adds to the fitting cost. They work well in modern, minimal bathrooms and save a small amount of floor space. The pan height can be set to suit the user - a benefit for taller people or those with mobility needs. Our wall-hung vs floor-mounted guide compares these options across all bathroom fixtures. For a head-to-head on the two concealed-cistern styles, read wall-hung vs back-to-wall toilet . Close coupled toilets A close coupled toilet has the cistern bolted directly on top of the pan. It is the most common type in existing Australian homes and the cheapest to buy and fit. The cistern is visible but sits right against the bowl. These are a good budget choice when the plumbing stays in the same place. They are simple to install, easy to repair and widely available. The trade-off is a bulkier look compared to a back to wall or wall-hung model. Water ratings and WELS Every toilet sold in Australia carries a WELS (Water Efficiency Labelling and Standards) star rating. A 4-star dual-flush toilet uses about 4.5 litres on a full flush and 3 litres on a half flush. results.bodyText: Planning and cost Underfloor heating in a bathroom: worth the cost? What underfloor heating costs during a bathroom renovation, how it works, whether it is worth it, and why the renovation is the right time to install it. Book a free on-site measure Call 0411 752 334 Published 3 October 2026 Reading time 4 min read The short answer If you are already renovating the bathroom and the floor is being stripped, underfloor heating is one of the most affordable comfort upgrades you can add. The cost is modest - typically $600 to $1,500 installed for a standard bathroom - and it runs for decades with almost no maintenance. The time to install it is during the renovation, when the floor is open and the electrician is already on site. Adding it later means lifting tiles, which is costly and disruptive. How it works Electric underfloor heating uses a thin heating mat or cable laid on the screed before the tiles go on. The mat sits between the waterproofing membrane and the tile adhesive. A thermostat on the wall controls the temperature and the schedule. The system heats the tile surface, not the air. You feel the warmth through your feet. It does not replace a room heater in cold climates, but in Sydney it takes the chill off a tile floor in the morning and makes the room noticeably more comfortable from autumn through spring. What it costs For a standard bathroom of 3 to 9 square metres, expect to pay $600 to $1,500 installed, including a programmable thermostat. The heating mat itself is the smaller part of the cost. The electrician's time to lay the mat, connect the thermostat and test the system is the larger part. Running costs are low. A typical bathroom heating mat draws 150 to 300 watts - similar to a couple of light bulbs. Running it for an hour in the morning costs a few cents. Over a full winter, the total running cost for most bathrooms is less than $30. Electric vs hydronic Electric heating mats are the standard choice for bathroom renovations. They are thin, easy to install under tiles, and work independently of the home's heating system. They suit rooms up to about 15 square metres. Hydronic underfloor heating circulates warm water through pipes in the floor. It is more efficient for heating whole houses but is more complex and expensive to install. It is rarely practical for a single-room bathroom renovation because it needs a boiler or heat pump, piping and a manifold. For a bathroom renovation, electric is almost always the right choice. Installation during a renovation The heating mat is laid after the waterproofing membrane has been applied and cured. The electrician positions the mat according to the room layout - typically covering the floor area where you stand, avoiding the area under the toilet, vanity and any fixed cabinetry. The thermostat sensor is embedded in the floor between the mat cables. The thermostat itself is mounted on the wall at switch height. The wiring connects to a dedicated circuit in the switchboard. The tiles go on top of the mat using a flexible tile adhesive. The system is not switched on until the adhesive has fully cured - usually seven days after tiling. What to consider Underfloor heating works best under tile and stone. These materials conduct heat well and feel warm underfoot. It is less effective under vinyl or timber, which insulate rather than conduct. The heating mat adds a small amount of height to the floor - typically 3 to 4 millimetres. In most renovations this is absorbed into the tile bed and makes no practical difference. If the bathroom has a timber subfloor, check that the heating mat is compatible. Most electric mats are rated for use on timber and concrete substrates, but the manufacturer's instructions should be followed. How ETR handles underfloor heating Underfloor heating is discussed at the on-site measure. If you want it, it is included in the written scope and the electrical rough-in. The mat is laid after demolition and waterproofing, before tiling. Every bathroom is waterproofed to AS 3740 with a compliance certificate. The underfloor heating sits on top of the membrane and does not affect the waterproofing. A free on-site measure anywhere in Sydney is the right starting point. acceptedAnswer.text: Generally, yes. A curbless entry, a built-in seat and grab bars make the room safer and easier to use. If you are planning to age in place, a walk-in shower is the more practical long-term choice.

results.bodyText: Compare your options Walk-in shower vs bathtub: how to choose during a bathroom renovation How to decide between a walk-in shower and a bathtub when you are renovating - what suits your space, your household and your resale position. Book a free on-site measure Call 0411 752 334 Published 2 October 2026 Reading time 4 min read Why this decision matters more than most fixture choices The shower-or-bath question is one of the first layout decisions in a bathroom renovation and one of the hardest to change later. It sets the floor plan, the plumbing positions, the waterproofing footprint and the way the room feels to use every day. There is no universally right answer. The choice depends on who uses the room, how much space you have, whether you plan to sell, and what you actually do in the bathroom on a weekday morning. When a walk-in shower makes the most sense A walk-in shower suits bathrooms where space is tight, access needs to be easy, or the household simply does not use a bath. In a compact room - say 1.5 by 2.4 metres - removing the bath and fitting a full-width shower opens the floor plan and gives more room to move. Walk-in showers are also the stronger choice for accessibility. A curbless entry, a built-in seat and grab bars make the room safer for older adults and anyone with limited mobility. If you are planning to stay in the home long term, this is worth considering now rather than retrofitting later - our accessible bathroom guide covers the full range of features. From a cleaning standpoint, a frameless glass shower with wall-to-wall tiling is simpler to maintain than a bath surround with grout joints, silicone seals and hard-to-reach corners. When a bathtub still adds value If there are young children in the home, a bath is practical - bathing a toddler in a shower is awkward at best. Families with children under five or six generally benefit from keeping at least one bath in the house. A freestanding bath in a larger bathroom can also serve as a design centrepiece. In rooms with higher ceilings and enough floor area, the bath anchors the space and adds a sense of proportion that a shower alone does not. For resale, the general guidance is to keep at least one bathtub in a family home. Buyers with children expect it, and removing every bath from a three- or four-bedroom house can narrow the buyer pool. If the home has two bathrooms, converting one to a walk-in shower while keeping the bath in the other is a common and practical split. Space and layout considerations A standard bath takes up roughly 1,700 by 750 millimetres of floor space. A walk-in shower can work in a smaller footprint - as little as 900 by 900 millimetres, though 1,000 by 1,200 or wider is more comfortable. In a bathroom under four square metres, the bath often dominates the room and leaves little space for the vanity and toilet. Replacing it with a shower and reclaiming that floor area can make the whole room feel larger and more functional - see our guide to small bathroom renovations for more layout ideas. Layout also affects plumbing. Moving the waste position from a bath to a shower (or vice versa) is straightforward in a full renovation where the floor is being stripped and re-waterproofed, but it adds cost if you are trying to do it as a standalone job. What about a shower-over-bath? A shower-over-bath is the compromise most Australians grew up with. It gives you both options in one footprint, which matters when the bathroom is too small for separate fixtures. The trade-off is that neither function works as well as a dedicated version. The shower screen is usually a single panel rather than a full enclosure, water hits the bath surround at an angle, and stepping over the bath edge is less accessible than a curbless shower entry. If the room genuinely cannot fit both a separate shower and a bath, a shower-over-bath is a reasonable solution. If it can, dedicated fixtures will feel better to use and look cleaner. Cost difference between a shower and a bath In a full renovation where the room is stripped back anyway, the cost difference between installing a walk-in shower and installing a bath is mostly in the fixtures and the tiling area, not in the labour or waterproofing - both need a compliant membrane either way. A freestanding bath adds the cost of the bath itself (typically $800 to $3,000 depending on material and brand) plus the floor waste and mixer. A walk-in shower adds the cost of the shower screen (a frameless panel runs $600 to $1,500 installed), the showerhead and mixer, and any niche or seat tiling. The layout decision should be made before the quote, because it affects the floor plan, the tile quantities and the plumbing positions. ETR's packages start from $18,000 for a Basic renovation in a small bathroom, and the fixture choice is part of the selections process. How to decide Ask four questions. Does anyone in the household need or regularly use a bath? Is this the only bathroom in the home? Are you planning to sell within a few years? Is the room large enough to fit both comfortably? If nobody uses the bath and the home has more than one bathroom, a walk-in shower is usually the better use of the space. If young children are in the picture or resale is the priority in a single-bathroom home, keep the bath. The on-site measure is the right time to work through this. The room dimensions, the plumbing positions and the household's actual use all feed into the decision, and the written scope locks it in before work starts. paragraphs: How to decide between a walk-in shower and a bathtub when you are renovating - what suits your space, your household and your resale position.

The shower-or-bath question is one of the first layout decisions in a bathroom renovation and one of the hardest to change later. It sets the floor plan, the plumbing positions, the waterproofing footprint and the way the room feels to use every day.
There is no universally right answer. The choice depends on who uses the room, how much space you have, whether you plan to sell, and what you actually do in the bathroom on a weekday morning.

A walk-in shower suits bathrooms where space is tight, access needs to be easy, or the household simply does not use a bath. In a compact room - say 1.5 by 2.4 metres - removing the bath and fitting a full-width shower opens the floor plan and gives more room to move.

Walk-in showers are also the stronger choice for accessibility. A curbless entry, a built-in seat and grab bars make the room safer for older adults and anyone with limited mobility. If you are planning to stay in the home long term, this is worth considering now rather than retrofitting later - our accessible bathroom guide covers the full range of features.
From a cleaning standpoint, a frameless glass shower with wall-to-wall tiling is simpler to maintain than a bath surround with grout joints, silicone seals and hard-to-reach corners.

If there are young children in the home, a bath is practical - bathing a toddler in a shower is awkward at best. Families with children under five or six generally benefit from keeping at least one bath in the house.

A freestanding bath in a larger bathroom can also serve as a design centrepiece. In rooms with higher ceilings and enough floor area, the bath anchors the space and adds a sense of proportion that a shower alone does not.

For resale, the general guidance is to keep at least one bathtub in a family home. Buyers with children expect it, and removing every bath from a three- or four-bedroom house can narrow the buyer pool. If the home has two bathrooms, converting one to a walk-in shower while keeping the bath in the other is a common and practical split.

A standard bath takes up roughly 1,700 by 750 millimetres of floor space. A walk-in shower can work in a smaller footprint - as little as 900 by 900 millimetres, though 1,000 by 1,200 or wider is more comfortable.

In a bathroom under four square metres, the bath often dominates the room and leaves little space for the vanity and toilet. Replacing it with a shower and reclaiming that floor area can make the whole room feel larger and more functional - see our guide to small bathroom renovations for more layout ideas.

Layout also affects plumbing. Moving the waste position from a bath to a shower (or vice versa) is straightforward in a full renovation where the floor is being stripped and re-waterproofed, but it adds cost if you are trying to do it as a standalone job.
A shower-over-bath is the compromise most Australians grew up with. It gives you both options in one footprint, which matters when the bathroom is too small for separate fixtures.

The trade-off is that neither function works as well as a dedicated version. The shower screen is usually a single panel rather than a full enclosure, water hits the bath surround at an angle, and stepping over the bath edge is less accessible than a curbless shower entry.
If the room genuinely cannot fit both a separate shower and a bath, a shower-over-bath is a reasonable solution. If it can, dedicated fixtures will feel better to use and look cleaner.

In a full renovation where the room is stripped back anyway, the cost difference between installing a walk-in shower and installing a bath is mostly in the fixtures and the tiling area, not in the labour or waterproofing - both need a compliant membrane either way.

A freestanding bath adds the cost of the bath itself (typically $800 to $3,000 depending on material and brand) plus the floor waste and mixer. A walk-in shower adds the cost of the shower screen (a frameless panel runs $600 to $1,500 installed), the showerhead and mixer, and any niche or seat tiling.

The layout decision should be made before the quote, because it affects the floor plan, the tile quantities and the plumbing positions. ETR's packages start from $18,000 for a Basic renovation in a small bathroom, and the fixture choice is part of the selections process.

Ask four questions. Does anyone in the household need or regularly use a bath? Is this the only bathroom in the home? Are you planning to sell within a few years? Is the room large enough to fit both comfortably?

If nobody uses the bath and the home has more than one bathroom, a walk-in shower is usually the better use of the space. If young children are in the picture or resale is the priority in a single-bathroom home, keep the bath.

The on-site measure is the right time to work through this. The room dimensions, the plumbing positions and the household's actual use all feed into the decision, and the written scope locks it in before work starts.

mainEntity.name: Are wall-hung toilets harder to repair?

acceptedAnswer.text: The parts you use most, the flush button and the cistern workings, are reached through the flush plate on the wall. The pan can be unbolted from the frame. Repairs are usually fine, but any fault inside the wall is harder to reach than on a floor-standing toilet.

mainEntity.name: Does a wall-hung toilet need a special wall?

acceptedAnswer.text: It needs a carrier frame fixed to the floor and the wall structure, and enough wall depth to hold the frame. The wall is often built out to fit. This is planned at rough-in, before the tiles go on.

mainEntity.name: How much weight can a wall-hung toilet hold?

acceptedAnswer.text: The load rating comes from the frame maker. Ask to see the rating on the data sheet, and have the frame installed exactly as the maker directs.

mainEntity.name: Is a wall-faced toilet the same as a back-to-wall toilet?

acceptedAnswer.text: Both names describe a pan that sits against the wall instead of out from it. Some suppliers use the two names for the same pan. Check the product sheet before you order.

mainEntity.name: Can I swap a close-coupled toilet for a wall-hung one?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, but it is not a simple swap. The waste pipe moves into the wall and a frame is fitted, so it works best in a full renovation while the wall is open.

Book a free on-site measure Call 0411 752 334 Published 2 November 2026 Reading time 5 min read Quick answer Choose a wall-hung toilet if you want a clear floor and a pan set at a height that suits you. Choose a back-to-wall toilet if you want a clean look and a simpler fit. Most back-to-wall setups hide the cistern in the wall or a cabinet, so both can look tidy. The real difference is how the pan is held. A wall-hung pan hangs from a frame in the wall. A back-to-wall pan stands on the floor and sits against the wall. You also pick the pan height when the frame is fixed. Taller people often like a higher pan. The open floor lets a small ensuite read as larger, which helps in a tight room. The trade-off is that the whole pan hangs from the wall, so the fixing is only as good as the frame and the wall behind it. That is why the build-up matters more than the pan itself. Why choose a back-to-wall toilet? A back-to-wall pan stands on the floor, so the floor carries its weight. The wall frame, where there is one, only has to hold the cistern. mainEntity.name: Is a wet room more expensive than a standard bathroom?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not necessarily. The shower screen is removed from the scope, but the waterproofing area is larger and the floor preparation is more involved. In a compact bathroom, the costs roughly balance. In a larger room, the additional prep can add to the total.

mainEntity.name: Does the whole bathroom floor get wet in a wet room?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, the floor in the shower zone gets wet, and splash reaches further without a screen. A well-graded floor drains quickly, but towels, bath mats and items stored at floor level will get damp near the shower area.

mainEntity.name: Are wet rooms suitable for families with children?

acceptedAnswer.text: They can be, but a family bathroom where children use the floor may suit a defined shower zone better. A wet room in a second bathroom or ensuite is a practical alternative that keeps the family bathroom dry.

mainEntity.name: What tiles are best for a wet room floor?

acceptedAnswer.text: A tile rated P3 or higher for wet barefoot areas. Mosaics grip well because of the grout lines, and textured porcelain tiles offer a good balance between grip and easy cleaning. Avoid polished tiles on any wet room floor.

mainEntity.name: Do wet rooms need special waterproofing?

acceptedAnswer.text: The standard is the same - AS 3740 - but the waterproofed area is larger. The full floor and a minimum height up every wall must be sealed. Most wet rooms waterproof the walls to full height for complete protection.

What a wet room actually is, how it differs from a standard bathroom, and whether it suits your space, your household and your renovation budget. Book a free on-site measure Call 0411 752 334 Published 3 October 2026 Reading time 4 min read What a wet room actually is A wet room is a bathroom where the entire floor is waterproofed and graded to a drain, with no shower screen, no hob and no tray separating the shower from the rest of the room. The shower is part of the floor, not a contained enclosure. The idea is simple: the whole room handles water. In practice, that means the waterproofing, drainage and floor gradient need to be right across the full area, not just inside a shower recess. How it differs from a standard bathroom In a standard bathroom, the shower sits inside a defined wet zone - a hob at the floor, a screen on the sides, a tray underneath. The rest of the room stays dry. A wet room removes that boundary. The shower is open, the floor slopes to a drain, and the whole room is the wet zone. This changes the waterproofing scope. A standard bathroom waterproofs the shower area plus a set distance around it. A wet room waterproofs the full floor and a portion of every wall. The membrane area is larger, and the floor prep is more involved because the gradient must carry water to the drain from every part of the room. When a wet room makes sense Wet rooms work well in compact bathrooms where a shower screen would crowd the room. Removing the screen and hob opens up the floor and makes the space feel larger. A 1.5 by 2 metre bathroom that feels tight with a framed shower can feel open as a wet room. They also suit accessibility needs. A flat floor with no step and no screen to navigate around is easier for older adults, wheelchair users and anyone with limited mobility. Our accessible bathroom guide covers the full range of features that make a room safer. Wet rooms can also suit a second bathroom or ensuite where the room is small and the design can be simple. When a wet room may not be the right choice If the bathroom needs to stay dry between uses - for example, a family bathroom where children dress and undress on the floor - a wet room means the whole floor gets wet every time the shower runs. Towels, bath mats and a toilet roll holder near the shower zone will get damp. A wet room also means the toilet, vanity and any cabinetry are in the splash zone. Timber vanities and unsealed surfaces need to handle moisture, and storage at floor level gets wet unless it is raised or enclosed. If the room is large, a wet room can feel excessive. A spacious bathroom with a dedicated shower and a freestanding bath usually works better with a defined shower zone than as a fully open wet room. Waterproofing and drainage The waterproofing in a wet room is the same standard as any bathroom - AS 3740 - but it covers a larger area. The full floor, the junction between floor and walls, and a minimum height up every wall must be sealed. In practice, most wet rooms waterproof the walls to full height. The floor gradient is critical. The entire floor must fall toward the drain, typically at a gradient of 1 in 80 to 1 in 100. A linear drain along one wall simplifies the fall because the floor slopes in one direction. A central point drain needs a four-way fall, which is harder to set up cleanly with large tiles. Every wet room ETR builds is waterproofed to AS 3740 with a compliance certificate. Tile and finish considerations Tile choice matters more in a wet room because the whole floor gets wet. A tile rated P3 or higher for wet barefoot areas reduces slip risk. Mosaics grip well because of the grout lines, but they are harder to clean. A textured porcelain tile is a good middle ground. Large-format tiles on a graded floor need careful cutting and layout. The gradient creates a slight curve across the surface, and a 600 by 600 tile will show lippage if the screed is not perfect. Smaller tiles follow the fall more easily. Our tiling and finishes guide covers tile formats in more detail. Cost considerations A wet room does not automatically cost more than a standard bathroom. The shower screen is removed from the scope, which saves $600 to $1,500. But the waterproofing area is larger, the floor preparation is more involved, and the screed needs to be set to a precise gradient across the full room. In a compact bathroom, those costs roughly balance. In a larger room, the additional waterproofing and screed work can add to the total. Tile choice matters more in a wet room because the whole floor gets wet. A tile rated P3 or higher for wet barefoot areas reduces slip risk. Mosaics grip well because of the grout lines, but they are harder to clean. A textured porcelain tile is a good middle ground.

Large-format tiles on a graded floor need careful cutting and layout. The gradient creates a slight curve across the surface, and a 600 by 600 tile will show lippage if the screed is not perfect. Smaller tiles follow the fall more easily. Our tiling and finishes guide covers tile formats in more detail.

A wet room does not automatically cost more than a standard bathroom. The shower screen is removed from the scope, which saves $600 to $1,500. But the waterproofing area is larger, the floor preparation is more involved, and the screed needs to be set to a precise gradient across the full room.

In a compact bathroom, those costs roughly balance. In a larger room, the additional waterproofing and screed work can add to the total. ETR's packages start from $18,000 for a Basic renovation - the on-site measure confirms whether a wet room layout suits the room and the budget.

mainEntity.name: How much does a bathroom renovation cost in Sydney?

acceptedAnswer.text: With Elite Touch, a bathroom renovation starts from $18,000 for a small bathroom (about 1.5 × 1.8 × 2.4 m, our Basic package), from $25,000 for a bathroom about 1.8 × 2.4 × 2.4 m (Standard), or from $30,000 for a bathroom about 2.4 × 2.4 × 2.4 m (Premium). Every figure is a starting price - you get a fixed-scope written quote after a free on-site measure.

mainEntity.name: Is $30,000 the minimum for a bathroom renovation?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. $30,000 is where our Premium package starts, for a bathroom about 2.4 × 2.4 × 2.4 m with a freestanding bath and heated flooring. Our Basic package starts from $18,000, for a bathroom around 1.5 × 1.8 × 2.4 m, and still includes full demolition, AS 3740 waterproofing, new tiling and all new fittings.

mainEntity.name: What's included in the price?

acceptedAnswer.text: Every package includes demolition, waterproofing to Australian Standards, new tiling, a custom shower screen, all new fittings and a final clean. The tiers differ in how much of the bathroom is tiled and which fittings are included - not the standard of work.

mainEntity.name: Do you offer complete bathroom renovation packages?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. The Basic, Standard and Premium packages are complete bathroom renovation starting scopes. Each one includes demolition, waterproofing, tiling, fitting installation and final clean-up. The package is not a fixed quote until the room is measured and the written scope is agreed.

mainEntity.name: Is the price fixed once work starts?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. You get a fixed-scope written quote after a free on-site measure, before any work begins. If your bathroom's size or scope differs from a package, we tell you at the measure - never after demolition.

mainEntity.name: How long does a bathroom renovation take?

acceptedAnswer.text: A full renovation on the same footprint usually takes 3–4 weeks. A premium build with natural stone and custom joinery takes 5–6 weeks, and a reconfiguration that moves walls or fixtures takes 5–7 weeks.
